description:
Samsung made about $80 billion in three months, and its phone business still lost money. 📱🔥

Before it made phones, TVs or chips, Samsung sold dried fish. This video follows the whole wild ride: a 1938 shop in Daegu, a war, a deal with a general, a chip bet everyone called crazy, the day the chairman set 150,000 of his own phones on fire, the Apple war, exploding batteries, a family in and out of court, and a comeback powered by AI.

title: The  Rise and Fall of Blockbuster in 10 Minutes
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Everyone says Netflix killed Blockbuster. That's not really what happened.

In 2000, Netflix offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for $50 million and got turned down. That part is true. But a few years later, Blockbuster had a hybrid DVD-by-mail and in-store service that genuinely had Netflix worried. So why did the company with 9,000 stores and nearly $6 billion a year in revenue still end up as one store in Bend, Oregon?

This is the story of a software guy who saw video rentals as a data problem, a garbage tycoon who opened a store every 17 hours, a business that made $800 million a year from late fees, a streaming deal with Enron, a boardroom war with Carl Icahn, and a last store that still charges late fees today.

What do you think? Could Blockbuster have survived if John Antioco had stayed? Tell us in the comments.

SOURCES

description:

description:
Walmart history and the Sam Walton story: how Walmart started as a five and dime in a town of 3,000 people and became the first traditional retailer worth 1 trillion dollars, built on a truck route and the few cents you would cross a parking lot to save. This history of Walmart covers Sam Walton, how Walmart was made, the Walmart success story, its distribution network, the Walmart vs Amazon rivalry, and the future of personalized pricing.

In its last fiscal year, Walmart brought in more than $713 billion and employed around 2.1 million people, and about 9 in 10 Americans live within 10 miles of a store. In 2026 it crossed a $1 trillion market value for the first time, the same week a former hourly worker, John Furner, became CEO.

description:
The history of Amazon and the Jeff Bezos story: how Amazon started as a bookstore in a garage and became a 3 trillion dollar company built on one thing, your impatience. This Amazon history documentary covers Jeff Bezos, why Amazon is so successful, the dot-com bubble, the Amazon flywheel, Amazon Prime, Amazon Web Services, the Kindle, Alexa, Whole Foods, and the FTC antitrust case.

When Amazon went public in 1997, the entire company was valued at about $438 million. Today it brings in more than $200 billion a quarter and employs around 1.5 million people, and in August 2026 its market cap passed $3 trillion for the first time, while most of its operating profit now comes from AWS, not the store.

This documentary follows the complete history of Amazon: Jeff Bezos's childhood and his grandfather's ranch in Cotulla, Texas, Operation Pedro Pan, D. E. Shaw and the regret minimization framework, why Bezos chose books, the drive to Seattle, Cadabra and Relentless.com, the Bellevue garage and the door desk, the order bell, the 1997 IPO and the first shareholder letter, Amazon.bomb, Person of the Year, the 1-Click patent, the dot-com crash, the $672 million bond sale that saved Amazon, the first profit, the flywheel napkin, the third-party marketplace, Amazon Prime, the AWS origin myth, the six-page memo, the Kindle, the fall of Borders, Kiva robots, the Fire Phone, Alexa and the Echo, the Whole Foods deal, the $1 trillion milestone and HQ2, Andy Jassy, the Amazon Labor Union, the FTC's Iliad and Project Nessie allegations, the $2.5 billion Prime settlement, Amazon Leo, record 2026 earnings, the $3 trillion market cap, the Miami cargo crash, Prime refunds, and the 2027 monopoly trial.

A garage could not hold it. A market collapse could not kill it. The giants that laughed at it could not outlast it. And in 2026, Amazon's oldest bet is the thing on trial: not a product, but you.
